overview: This bill sets up a federal effort to restore white oak trees, a valuable hardwood used for lumber, barrels and wildlife habitat, whose numbers are not regrowing well in many forests. It formally recognizes a voluntary coalition of governments, tribes and private groups to coordinate restoration and recommend policy changes, and directs the Forest Service and the Interior Department to each run five pilot restoration projects on federal land, after Interior assesses where white oak grows on its lands. It creates a white oak grant and technical assistance program run with the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation, a national strategy to address shortages of tree seedlings at nurseries, a research partnership with tribes and colleges, and an Agriculture Department initiative to help private landowners regrow white oak. Most of these authorities would end after seven years. As of January 8, 2026, the House Natural Resources Committee had approved an amended version.
for: Supporters say coordinated action is needed to reverse the decline of an economically and ecologically important tree, and the bill builds on existing partnerships and programs rather than creating new bureaucracy.
against: Critics say the bill adds new federal programs, pilots and reporting duties focused on a single tree species, which could pull limited agency staff and money from other forest priorities.
